question: After rotation, the inner product between a data vector and its quantized vector is about 0.8 in high dimensions. What does this number mean?
options: The code is wrong in 20% of the bits
The estimator is accurate to within 0.2
The quantized vector is a unit vector at roughly 37 degrees from the data vector, so using it directly would shrink inner products
Only 80% of vectors get a valid code
explain: Both are unit vectors and their cosine is about 0.8 (about 37 degrees). Lesson 4 shows why treating o-bar as if it were o is biased, and how dividing by this stored 0.8-ish value fixes it.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Why replicas need consensus, and why majorities work
question: You run a 3-server cluster and add a fourth server for extra safety. How many simultaneous server failures can the cluster now survive while staying available?
options: 1, the same as before
2, one more than before
3, since one server is enough to serve reads
0, because 4 cannot form a majority
explain: With n = 4 the majority is 3, so only 1 server may be down. You added replication cost (one more copy on every write) without improving availability. Go to 5 servers to tolerate 2 failures.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Consensus in production: reads, membership, timeouts
question: A team switches to lease-based reads to cut read latency. Under which condition can a client now see stale data?
options: When a follower's disk is slow
When the old leader's clock runs slow, so it keeps serving reads after a new leader has been elected
When two clients read the same key at once
Never; leases are as safe as ReadIndex
explain: A lease assumes the leader's sense of elapsed time matches the followers'. If its clock is slow or the process pauses, it may believe the lease is still valid after followers have timed out and elected someone else, and serve stale data. ReadIndex avoids this by checking with a majority on every batch of reads.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Prompting the generator to answer with citations
question: A statement cites [2][5]. Passage [5] alone entails it; [2] alone does not, and [5] without [2] still entails it. How does ALCE score this?
options: Citation recall 1; citation [2] counts as irrelevant, lowering precision
Citation recall 0, because [2] does not support the statement
Citation recall 1 and precision 1, since the statement is supported
Citation recall 0.5, one supporting passage out of two
explain: Recall asks whether the concatenation of cited passages entails the statement: yes, thanks to [5]. Precision checks each citation: [2] neither supports alone nor is needed with the others, so it is irrelevant.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: What a ranker sees: one feature vector per query-document pair
question: Why do LETOR and MSLR compute BM25 separately on body, anchor, title and URL instead of once on the whole page?
options: A match in the title and a match in the body are different evidence, and separate features let the model learn a weight for each
BM25 cannot be computed on long documents
It makes the index smaller
Search engines are required to by the TREC rules
explain: Per-field (per-stream) scores keep the evidence separate. A model can then learn that a title match is worth more than a body match for this collection, which a single whole-document score cannot express.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Feature logging: train on exactly the numbers you serve
question: A team logs only document ids and query strings, then recomputes all features nightly for training. Which feature is most at risk of skew?
options: URL length
Number of query terms
Freshness computed from age relative to now
Whether the title contains a query term
explain: URL length, query term count and title containment are stable for a fixed document and query. Freshness relative to now is recomputed hours or days later, so every training example looks older than it was when the user saw it.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Three runs, seven verdicts: when metrics disagree
question: For a first-stage retriever whose top 100 candidates are passed to a cross-encoder reranker, which metric best measures the retriever?
options: RR, since users only look at the first result
nDCG@10 with exponential gain
R@100, the share of relevant documents that make it into the candidate set
explain: The reranker can only reorder what the retriever passes on, so the retriever's job is coverage at depth 100. Order inside the 100 matters little because the reranker rescores them. Top-heavy metrics such as RR, P@1 or nDCG@10 belong to the final ranking.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Queue pairs, work requests and the completion queue
question: A program posts receive buffers and sends but never calls `ibv_poll_cq` on a busy CQ. What happens according to the verbs documentation?
options: Old CQEs are silently overwritten and traffic continues
The NIC stops sending until the CQ has room, like TCP flow control
The kernel enlarges the CQ automatically
The CQ overruns: IBV_EVENT_CQ_ERR is raised and the CQ can no longer be used
explain: The ibv_poll_cq man page warns that you must consume completions fast enough to avoid overrun; an overrun triggers IBV_EVENT_CQ_ERR and the CQ becomes unusable, and the manual adds that its QPs get a fatal event. Size the CQ for the maximum number of outstanding signaled WRs and receives.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: InfiniBand, RoCEv2 and iWARP: what carries the packets
question: Why does RoCEv2 put a UDP header in front of the IB transport header?
options: UDP provides retransmission for RDMA
UDP is required for PFC to work
To make RoCEv2 compatible with iWARP
So routers and switches can hash flows across equal-cost paths (ECMP); IP provides routing
explain: The DCQCN paper: the IP header is needed for routing, while the UDP header is needed for ECMP. Reliability still comes from the IB transport in the NIC, not from UDP.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: The authoritative server and its fixed tick
question: A client sends "my position is (20, 10)" every frame and the server copies it into the world. What is the core problem?
options: It uses too much bandwidth
The server cannot interpolate it
WebSocket frames cannot carry positions
The client is authoritative over its own position, so a modified client can teleport or move through walls
explain: Trusting client-reported state defeats the authoritative design. The client should send intents (move right) and the server should compute the resulting position and reject impossible moves.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: From a sparse rating matrix to item-to-item recommendations
question: With plain cosine and blanks as 0, Space1 and Rom1 come out at +0.28 although fans of one rate the other 1 star. Why?
options: Cosine is undefined for rating data, so the value is noise
All ratings are positive, so any two items rated by the same users share direction; adjusted cosine removes each user's mean first
The users who rated both items gave them identical ratings
Rom1 has more ratings than Space1, which inflates the cosine
explain: With non-negative entries the cosine can never be negative. Subtracting each user's average rating (adjusted cosine) turns 'rated 1 by a sci-fi fan' into a negative number, and the similarity becomes -0.97.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Cold start: content for new items, bandits for new users
question: In LinUCB, an arm has never been shown. What is its score p for any context x?
options: 0, so it is never chosen until an exploration phase
alpha times the norm of x, since A is the identity and b is zero, so it is likely to be tried
Its popularity
Undefined until the arm gets one reward
explain: With A_a = I and b_a = 0, theta is 0 and the bonus is alpha sqrt(x^T x). Unseen arms therefore carry the largest uncertainty bonus, which is how LinUCB explores new items.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: How wrong is it? Corner noise, out-of-plane height, pixels
question: Your measured lengths have about 1 mm of scatter between photos. Which change most directly reduces corner-noise error?
options: Switch from a homography to the pixels-per-mm ratio
Print a larger marker and place the object within or close to its footprint
Increase JPEG compression to reduce noise
Use a marker dictionary with more IDs
explain: A 1 px corner error is a smaller fraction of a larger marker, and objects inside the reference footprint are interpolated, not extrapolated (0.24 mm versus 1.28 mm in the toy). Dictionary size affects ID confusion, not corner accuracy.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: How the planner chooses: join order search and row estimates
question: A query joins 14 tables listed in FROM with default settings. How does PostgreSQL search for a join order?
options: With the Genetic Query Optimizer, since 14 is at least geqo_threshold (12)
Exhaustive dynamic programming over all 14 tables
It joins them in the order written
It refuses to plan queries over 12 tables
explain: GEQO is used for queries with at least geqo_threshold FROM items, 12 by default. It finds a reasonable order quickly but not necessarily the best. Exhaustive search would cost too much planning time at this size.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Failures: sloppy quorums, hinted handoff and repair
question: Why does Dynamo accept the risk that a sloppy quorum's read and write sets may not overlap?
options: Because vector clocks make overlap unnecessary
Because it prefers accepting writes (an always-writeable cart) and reconciles divergent versions later
Because R + W > N still holds, so overlap is guaranteed anyway
Because hinted replicas are counted twice
explain: Dynamo is designed to be always writeable: rejecting an add-to-cart is worse than briefly reading an old cart. It pays for that with possible divergence, which it detects with vector clocks and resolves at read time. That is the next lesson.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: KL regularization: a leash, not a cure
question: In the toy example, suppose the exploit D were common under the reference policy (reference probability 0.30 instead of 0.02). Compared with before, what does the KL penalty do?
options: It protects better, because D is now part of normal behavior
Nothing changes: the optimum depends only on the reward
It protects less: the policy can shift to D at little KL cost, so D dominates at a larger beta
It makes D impossible because KL is measured from the reference
explain: pi* is proportional to the reference probability times exp(r/beta). A larger reference probability for D means D wins at higher beta, with less KL spent. The penalty only resists moving away from the reference; it gives no protection against behavior the reference already does.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: The long tail: why one response can idle a whole cluster
question: A colleague proposes doubling the number of rollout engines, each still decoding a share of one synchronous batch, to fix 51% engine idleness. What is the main flaw?
options: More engines need more weight-sync bandwidth, which is the real bottleneck
Doubling engines doubles the length of every response
Engines cannot run in parallel on one batch
The idle time is set by the longest response, and one response cannot be split across engines, so the phase still lasts as long as that response
explain: Autoregressive decoding of one response is sequential. Adding engines shortens the time to finish the short responses, but the phase still waits for the longest one, so idleness goes up. verl's fully async docs make the same point: in the colocated case, adding rollout resources cannot remove long-tail idleness.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Why a kernel is limited by its slowest resource
question: A kernel does 2 GFLOP and moves 4 GB on an H100 (989.5 TFLOP/s BF16, 3.35 TB/s). Which change would speed it up the most?
options: Fusing it with the next kernel so its output never goes to DRAM
Switching from BF16 to FP8 Tensor Cores to double the math rate
Raising the SM clock to increase peak FLOP/s
Unrolling the inner loop to improve instruction level parallelism
explain: Math time is 2 GFLOP / 989.5 TFLOP/s = 2 us, memory time is 4 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 1,194 us. The kernel is memory bound, so only cutting bytes (fusion keeps intermediates on chip) helps. Every option that speeds up math leaves the 1,194 us untouched.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Walking the dependency graph to the anomalous frontier
question: Pricing is anomalous and so is catalog, which pricing calls. A junior engineer proposes rolling back pricing, since pricing is where the user-visible errors are counted. What does the frontier rule say?
options: Roll back pricing: it is the service returning errors, so it owns the symptom
Roll back both at once to save time
Pricing's anomaly is already explained by its anomalous dependency, so it is not a candidate until catalog is ruled out
Neither is a candidate, because both are anomalous
explain: The frontier keeps only anomalous nodes whose dependencies are healthy. Pricing's slowness is fully accounted for by waiting on catalog, and rolling back pricing changes nothing about the catalog queue while adding a second change to reason about. Rolling back both at once also destroys your ability to attribute the recovery to either one.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Why fuse ranks instead of scores
question: A new BM25 build multiplies every BM25 score by 3 (same order). What happens to the RRF-fused list?
options: Nothing: ranks are unchanged, so every RRF score is unchanged
BM25 now dominates the fusion, like the raw sum
Dense-only documents rise because BM25 is now relatively noisier
The fused list changes only if k is smaller than 3
explain: RRF reads only r(d). Any monotone transformation of one system's scores leaves its ranks, and therefore the fused list, identical. A raw score sum would change; min-max would not change in this case either, but would under a non-linear transform.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Bindings, helpers, abstractions: the layers under a Rust driver
question: A colleague's build fails: `bindings::spin_lock` does not exist even though `spin_lock()` is used all over the C code. Most likely cause?
options: The bindings crate only includes headers listed in `rust/helpers/`
Rust code may not take spinlocks
`spin_lock` is a macro or inline function in C, so bindgen emits no callable symbol; a `rust/helpers/` wrapper is needed
bindgen only runs when `CLIPPY=1` is set
explain: bindgen generates declarations for real functions and types it finds in the headers included from `rust/bindings/bindings_helper.h`. For C inline functions and non-trivial macros the docs say to add a small wrapper to `rust/helpers/`, exactly like `rust_helper_mutex_lock`.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: What Rust in the kernel does not prevent, and what it costs
question: Which of these bugs does the safe `Mutex`/`Guard` API rule out at compile time in a driver that uses no `unsafe`?
options: Taking lock A then B in one path and B then A in another (ABBA deadlock)
Returning from an error path while the mutex is still held
Calling a sleeping function while holding a spinlock
Holding the lock for too long and hurting latency
explain: The guard's `Drop` unlocks on every exit path. Lock ordering is still checked at runtime by lockdep, sleeping in atomic context needs extra tooling such as klint, and latency is a design question no type system answers.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Worked example: weighted vtime fairness in a few lines of BPF
question: You remove the clamp from scx_simple's enqueue. Which symptom appears first?
options: CPU-bound tasks starve each other in a round-robin cycle
A task waking from a long sleep runs back to back for about as long as it slept, starving CPU-bound tasks
The verifier rejects the program because vtime can underflow
Nice values stop having any effect
explain: A sleeper's vtime stays where it was, while running tasks keep advancing. Without the cap, the waker is far behind and wins every pick until it catches up. If that exceeds the watchdog timeout, the scheduler could even be unloaded for stalling others.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: When the filter lies: lucky answers, proxy rewards, overfitting
question: In ReST, reward model scores keep rising with every Grow step, but human raters prefer the model after one Grow step. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The policy is increasingly exploiting errors in the learned reward model, a proxy for human judgment
Human raters are noisier than the reward model, so their results should be ignored
The Improve thresholds were set too low
Translation quality cannot improve after one Grow step for any method
explain: The reward model is only a proxy. Optimizing a proxy harder eventually finds outputs it overrates. The ReST authors say exactly this and suggest periodically refreshing the reward model with human labels on the newest policy's outputs.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: What is safe to cache: scoping, context and invalidation
question: Your support bot caches answers for 24 hours with a TTL that refreshes on every hit, as RedisVL does when a TTL is set. The refund policy changes today. What happens to the popular cached answer "Refunds are accepted within 30 days"?
options: It expires within 24 hours of the change
It may never expire, because every hit resets its TTL; you must delete it or bump a version tag
Redis detects that the source changed and evicts it
It expires at midnight
explain: A TTL that refreshes on access measures time since last use, not time since creation. A frequently asked question keeps getting hit and never expires. Policy-dependent answers need explicit invalidation: delete by source id or change the scope version.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: LM programs: why the runtime should see the whole program
question: Why does the interpreter send the shared prefix to the runtime before the fork branches?
options: So that the prefix is computed and inserted into the radix tree once; branches arriving together would otherwise each find nothing cached and each prefill it
Because the runtime cannot accept prompts longer than the prefix
To let the runtime pick a different model for each branch
Because RadixAttention only works when requests arrive one at a time
explain: If both branches arrive at the same moment with nothing cached, each matches zero tokens and each computes the shared part. The paper calls the fix a frontend hint: it simplifies runtime matching and is one of the co-design benefits in its ablation.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Turning a road map into a weighted directed graph
question: In the toy graph, a planner picks the route with the fewest roads and breaks ties arbitrarily. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing; fewest roads always means fastest when weights are minutes
It may return S, C, F, T (14 min) even though S, D, F, T takes 9 min
It cannot find any route, because BFS ignores weights entirely
It always returns the slowest 3-road route
explain: Three routes tie at 3 roads (9, 10 and 14 minutes). Hop count ignores weights, so any of them can come out. We need an algorithm that compares accumulated minutes, which is exactly what Dijkstra's algorithm does.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
question: A travel time function says: leave at 08:05 and arrive at 08:30.6, or leave at 08:10 and arrive at 08:27.4. What does this violate, and why does it matter?
options: Admissibility; A* would overestimate
Nonnegative weights; travel times went negative
FIFO; waiting would beat leaving now, which breaks the label-setting search for earliest arrival
Turn restrictions; the profile is missing a penalty
explain: Leaving later and arriving earlier violates FIFO. Then arriving at a node as early as possible no longer guarantees arriving as early as possible further along, so a settled earliest-arrival label can be wrong. Dijkstra-style time-dependent search assumes FIFO, and the survey notes that other settings are studied separately.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: IIR filters, zero-phase filtering and real sensor data
question: A drone's control loop needs a filtered gyro reading every 1 ms. Someone proposes `sosfiltfilt` because it has zero phase delay. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; zero phase is ideal for control
sosfiltfilt only works on FIR filters
sosfiltfilt runs the filter backward from the end of the signal, so it needs future samples and cannot run in real time
sosfiltfilt halves the filter order, so it filters too weakly
explain: The backward pass starts from the last sample, which a real-time loop does not have yet. Real-time systems must use a causal filter (sosfilt, or an FIR) and accept or compensate its delay. Forward-backward filtering doubles the effective order; it does not halve it.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Masks instead of branches: compares, blends and AVX-512
question: In AVX-512, `r = _mm512_mask_add_ps(src, k, a, b)` with k = 0x0003. What are lanes 0 and 5 of r?
options: Lane 0 = a0 + b0, lane 5 = 0
Lane 0 = src0, lane 5 = a5 + b5
Both lanes are a + b; k only affects stores
Lane 0 = a0 + b0, lane 5 = src5
explain: 0x0003 sets bits 0 and 1, so lanes 0 and 1 get a + b. The mask_ form is merge masking: inactive lanes copy src. The maskz_ form would have produced 0 in lane 5.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Why a general-purpose heap wastes memory
question: Why does a program not simply call `mmap` for every 24-byte object?
options: mmap cannot return memory smaller than a page, and each call is a system call, so it is both wasteful and slow
mmap memory cannot be written to until it is passed through malloc
mmap always returns memory on a different NUMA node
mmap regions are freed automatically after one function returns
explain: mmap works in whole pages (4 KiB on typical x86-64) and costs a kernel entry per call. An allocator amortizes both costs by carving many small objects out of one mapping.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Three modules, one loop: how slime is laid out
question: You want to raise SGLang's KV cache budget inside a slime run. SGLang's own flag is `--mem-fraction-static`. What do you pass to slime's train.py?
options: `--sglang-mem-fraction-static 0.8`
`--mem-fraction-static 0.8`, since slime forwards unknown flags
Nothing: slime fixes SGLang memory internally
`--rollout-mem-fraction 0.8`
explain: SGLang arguments are passed through with a `--sglang-` prefix. Unprefixed flags are interpreted as Megatron or slime arguments, and there is no slime-specific rollout memory flag.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Fully async rollout and the price of staleness
question: A teammate enables fully async rollout on a colocated 8-GPU job and sees no speedup. Why?
options: Fully async only works with PPO
The default --sglang-server-concurrency is too low
With colocation rollout and training share GPUs and must take turns, so there are no independent resources to overlap
Fully async requires delta weight sync
explain: The docs say fully async needs separate GPUs for meaningful overlap. On shared GPUs the phases still alternate, so the async bound does not apply.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Enforcing sparsity: L1, TopK and JumpReLU
question: An L1 SAE's latents look right on inspection, but its reconstructions are consistently a bit too short (smaller norm than x). What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Dead latents; resample them
The learning rate is too high; lower it
Shrinkage from the L1 penalty; use TopK, JumpReLU or a Gated SAE, or re-fit magnitudes on the chosen latents
The dictionary is too large; reduce M
explain: L1 pulls every active magnitude down by about lambda/2 (in the one-latent case), so x-hat is systematically small. Architectures that decouple selection from magnitude remove this bias.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: The semivariogram: measuring how similarity decays with distance
question: Your fitted variogram has a large nugget, almost equal to the sill. What does this say about your sensors?
options: Readings are strongly correlated at all distances, so interpolation will be very accurate
The range must be zero, so kriging cannot be run
Even very close sensors disagree about as much as distant ones, so spatial interpolation adds little over the mean
Close sensors always agree exactly
explain: The nugget is the semivariance as distance approaches zero. If it is almost the sill, nearby pairs differ about as much as unrelated pairs: the measurable spatial structure is weak (or dominated by measurement error), and kriging estimates approach the mean.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Why decoding is slow and why checking guesses is cheap
question: Which claim about speculative decoding is correct?
options: It speeds up decoding by letting a smaller model answer the easy prompts
It trades a small amount of quality for latency, like quantization
It produces the same output distribution as the target model and only changes how many target passes are needed
It only works with greedy decoding
explain: Both original papers prove the sampled tokens follow the target's distribution for any draft. Quality is unchanged; speed depends on how well the draft guesses. Lesson 3 covers sampling, not just greedy.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Drafting without a second model: Medusa heads and token trees
question: A tree-attention kernel accidentally uses the ordinary causal mask on the flattened tree. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; causal masking is a superset of tree masking
Only the position ids are off by one
The pass becomes slower but results are identical
Each node also attends to earlier sibling branches, so the target scores tokens in contexts that never occur and verification becomes wrong
explain: Under a causal mask 'think' would attend to 'It', 'is', 'was' and so on, a context that is not its real prefix. Its distribution is then wrong and so are the accept and reject decisions. The mask must restrict attention to ancestors.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Word error rate: alignments, normalization and fair comparisons
question: A reference has 10 words. The aligned hypothesis has 2 substitutions, 1 deletion and 3 insertions. What is the WER?
explain: WER = (S + D + I) / N = (2 + 1 + 3) / 10 = 60%. Dividing by the hypothesis length (12 words) would give 50%, a common bug. 30% forgets the insertions.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Walking an x86-64 page table, bit by bit
question: A program maps 1 GiB of memory and touches all of it with 4 KiB pages. Roughly how much memory do the last-level page tables alone take?
options: 4 KiB
64 KiB
2 MiB
1 GiB
explain: 1 GiB / 4 KiB = 262,144 PTEs at 8 bytes each = 2 MiB, which is 512 PTE tables of 4 KiB. With 2 MiB pages the same gigabyte needs just 512 PMD entries, one 4 KiB table.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Difference of means: building a vector from contrast pairs
question: In the toy example, the single-pair direction from pair 4 still classifies all eight activations correctly. Why prefer the mean difference anyway?
options: It is the only direction with unit length
It makes projections of negatives exactly zero
Single-pair vectors cannot be added to the residual stream
It is closer to the true concept direction (cosine 0.991 vs 0.891), so steering along it changes less of everything else
explain: Classification only needs the right sign. Steering adds the whole vector, including its off-concept components. Pair 4's direction has a larger share of noise, so adding it would also push unrelated dimensions. The averaged vector is cleaner.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Two clocks: why sensor readings arrive out of order
question: Which timestamp should you use to decide whether a machine overheated between 14:00:00 and 14:00:10?
options: Processing time at the stream processor
Kafka's append time for the record
The event time the sensor stamped on the reading
The time the database row was written
explain: Only the event time refers to when the physical measurement happened. The other three are processing times at different stages, each shifted by network and queueing delay.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
question: A consumer commits its Kafka offset immediately after reading a batch and before writing results. It crashes mid-write. What semantics did you get?
options: Exactly once
At least once
At most once: the batch's unwritten results are lost
No effect, Kafka rolls back the commit
explain: Committing before processing means on restart the consumer resumes after the batch; anything not yet written is never processed. Kafka's docs describe this as the at-most-once pattern.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Positional encoding, residuals and the full Transformer
question: Which sub-layer holds the most parameters in one base-model encoder layer?
options: Multi-head self-attention, because it has 8 heads
LayerNorm, because it has a gain and bias per dimension
The position-wise feed-forward network, about twice as many as attention
They are equal by design
explain: Attention: 4 x 512^2, about 1.05 million. FFN: 2 x 512 x 2048, about 2.10 million. LayerNorm has only 2 x 512 = 1,024 per instance. Heads split the attention width; they do not add parameters.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Document length normalization: what b controls
question: Under b = 0.75, avgdl = 20, k1 = 1.2, what is K = k1 x B for a 40-token document?
options: 1.2, the same as k1
2.4, because the document is twice the average
0.6, because long documents saturate sooner
explain: B = 0.25 + 0.75 x (40/20) = 1.75, so K = 1.2 x 1.75 = 2.1. It is not 2.4 because only the b share of B scales with length; the (1 - b) share stays fixed. A larger K means the long document needs more occurrences to reach the same factor, not fewer.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head
question: For GPT-2 small, roughly what share of all parameters sits in the MLPs?
options: About 10%
About 23%
About 45%
About 31%
explain: The MLPs have 8C^2 + 5C per block, twice attention's 4C^2 + 4C, totalling 56.67M of 124.44M, which is 45.5%. 23% is attention and 31% is the token embedding table.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Many inputs: partial derivatives and the gradient vector
question: A model has 7 billion parameters and a scalar loss. How many numbers are in the gradient of the loss?
options: 1, because the loss is a single number
7 billion, one partial derivative per parameter
About 49 billion billion (7 billion squared), one per pair of parameters
It depends on the batch size
explain: The gradient has one entry per input to the function: here, one partial derivative per parameter. Pairs of parameters appear in the matrix of second derivatives (the Hessian), which is far too large to form for such models.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: Expansion and quoting: why rm $f can delete the wrong files
question: In bash, `echo {1,2}-$((3+4))` prints what?
explain: Brace expansion runs first and makes two words, `1-$((3+4))` and `2-$((3+4))`. Arithmetic expansion then evaluates each to 7.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: From one-hot IDs to a trainable embedding table
question: Why do the dense vectors let a model generalize from cat to kitten when one-hot codes do not?
options: Dense vectors have more dimensions, so they hold more information
The dot product of two one-hot vectors is undefined
Nearby inputs produce nearby activations, so what the network learned for one word partly applies to the other
Dense vectors are normalized to length 1
explain: The downstream layers are smooth functions of their input. If kitten's vector is close to cat's, the network's output for kitten is close to its output for cat. One-hot codes have more dimensions, not fewer, and their dot products are well defined (just always 0).

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Beyond words: contrastive learning and failure modes
question: Your product catalog adds thousands of new item IDs every day, and the model uses one learned embedding row per ID. What problem should you expect for brand-new items?
options: Their rows are still at their random initialization because they have received no gradient, so their similarities are meaningless
None, embeddings generalize to any ID
They will all collapse to the zero vector
Their vectors will equal the average of all rows
explain: A row learns only when its ID appears in training. New IDs keep their random initial vectors (in PyTorch drawn from N(0, 1)). Systems handle this cold-start problem by building vectors from content features, the same idea fastText uses with character n-grams.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Batching: sharing each weight read across many users
question: Why does continuous batching improve throughput over static batching?
options: Finished requests free their slot right away and waiting requests join at the next step, so fewer slots sit idle
It makes each decode step faster
It removes the need for a KV cache
It runs prefill and decode on different GPUs
explain: The step time is unchanged; what changes is how full the batch is. Iteration-level scheduling refills slots every iteration instead of waiting for the longest request.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why memory is slow and how caches hide it
question: With a 3-cycle hit time and a 240-cycle miss penalty, what is the average access time at a 5% miss rate?
options: 12 cycles
15 cycles
243 cycles
8 cycles
explain: 3 + 0.05 x 240 = 3 + 12 = 15 cycles. Note that a 5% miss rate already makes the average access 5x slower than a hit: misses dominate.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Pretraining: next-token loss over trillions of tokens
question: Using C of about 6ND, a 7B-parameter model trained on 2 trillion tokens needs roughly how many FLOPs?
explain: 6 x 7e9 x 2e12 = 8.4e22. The rule ignores attention's context-length term, which Kaplan et al. note is small when the model width is large relative to the context.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward over-optimization, best-of-N and modern recipes
question: Best-of-N with N = 64 moves the output distribution how far from the base policy, by the analytic formula?
options: About 0.98 nats
About 4.16 nats
About 64 nats
About 3.18 nats
explain: log 64 - 63/64 = 4.159 - 0.984 = 3.175 nats. KL grows only logarithmically in N, which is why best-of-N is a gentle form of optimization.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity
question: N = 1,000,000 and a term has df = 1,000 and tf = 3 in a document. What is its weight with raw tf, and with sublinear tf 1 + log10(tf)?
explain: idf = log10(1,000,000 / 1,000) = 3. Raw: 3 x 3 = 9. Sublinear: (1 + log10 3) x 3 = 1.477 x 3 = 4.43. Sublinear scaling halves this weight here because three occurrences count as about 1.5.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Addresses and pointers: what int *p actually stores
question: On a 64-bit Linux or macOS machine, `char *c;` What are `sizeof c` and `sizeof *c`?
options: 1 and 1
8 and 8
8 and 1
1 and 8
explain: c is a pointer, and object pointers are 8 bytes on these platforms. *c is the char it would point to, which is 1 byte by definition. sizeof only looks at types, so it is fine to apply it even though c is uninitialized.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Who frees this memory? Ownership and drop
question: A function creates `let s = String::from("hi");` and returns normally without doing anything else with `s`. What happens to the heap bytes?
options: They are freed when the function returns, because `s` (the owner) goes out of scope and is dropped
They leak, because there is no explicit free
They are freed later when the garbage collector runs
They stay allocated until the program exits
explain: Rule 3: when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped, and dropping a String frees its heap buffer. Rust has no tracing garbage collector, and nothing waits until exit.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Lifetimes: tying a returned reference to its inputs
question: Which signature compiles **without** explicit lifetime annotations?
options: `fn pick(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str`
`fn make() -> &str`
`fn get(&self, key: &str) -> &str` (a method)
explain: Rule 3: the output takes the lifetime of `&self`. Options 1 and 4 have two input lifetimes and no receiver, and option 2 has no input lifetime at all, so elision cannot fill in the output in any of them (E0106).

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A matrix is a function that moves every vector
question: Is $f(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$ guaranteed to satisfy $f(2\mathbf{x}) = 2f(\mathbf{x})$ for every matrix $A$?
options: Only if A is square
Only if A is a rotation
Yes, for every matrix A
No, only if A has no negative entries
explain: Each output component is $\sum_j A_{ij}(2x_j) = 2\sum_j A_{ij}x_j$. Scaling passes through any matrix. This is half of the definition of linearity; the other half is $f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}) = f(\mathbf{x}) + f(\mathbf{y})$.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Mini-batches, cross-entropy gradients and the training loop
question: You switch from batch size 100 to batch size 10,000 on a huge dataset. What happens to one step's gradient estimate?
options: Its standard deviation drops about 10 times while each step costs about 100 times more
It becomes exact
Its standard deviation drops about 100 times, matching the 100 times extra compute
Nothing changes, because the minibatch gradient is unbiased at any batch size
explain: Standard error scales as $\sigma/\sqrt B$: $\sqrt{10000/100} = 10$. Unbiasedness means the estimate is right on average at any batch size, but its noise still depends on $B$. Only the full dataset gives the exact gradient.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The forward pass: layers as matrix multiplies
question: In the convention $z^l = W^l a^{l-1} + b^l$, what is the shape of $W^2$ for that 784-100-10 network?
explain: $W^l$ has one row per unit in layer $l$ and one column per unit in layer $l-1$: 10 output units by 100 hidden units.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Processes and limited direct execution
question: Why must the instruction that installs the trap table be privileged?
options: Because it is slow and should run only at boot
Because the trap table is stored on disk
Because a user process could otherwise point system calls and interrupts at its own code and take over the machine
Because user programs do not know the system-call numbers
explain: The trap table decides which code runs in kernel mode on every trap and interrupt. If a user program could install its own, it would run arbitrary code with full privilege, defeating all protection. So, like starting the timer, it is restricted to kernel mode.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
question: A model's training set has 1,000 emails: 300 are spam, and 240 of the spam emails contain the word "free". Of the 700 non-spam emails, 70 contain "free". What is P(spam | contains "free")?
options: 0.80, because 240 of 300 spam emails contain free
0.24, because 240 of 1,000 emails are spam with free
About 0.77, because 240 of the 310 emails containing free are spam
0.30, the base rate of spam
explain: Condition on the event you observed: restrict to the 240 + 70 = 310 emails containing "free", of which 240 are spam, so 240/310 = 0.774. Option A is P(free | spam), the reverse conditional, a very common mix-up that the next lesson is about.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Estimating parameters from data: maximum likelihood
question: A language model assigns probability 0.5 to every correct next token in a validation set. What is its average cross-entropy (natural log), and what does minimizing it on training data correspond to?
options: 0.5; minimizing the error rate
About 0.693; maximizing the likelihood of the training tokens
About 0.693; minimizing the variance of the predictions
1.0; maximizing accuracy
explain: Cross-entropy averages -log of the probability given to the correct token: -ln 0.5 = 0.693. Minimizing average negative log-likelihood over the training data is exactly maximum likelihood estimation of the model's parameters.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Fixed budget, best split: IsoFLOP curves
question: Under Chinchilla-style scaling (N and D each proportional to about $C^{0.5}$), your compute budget grows 10x. How should the model size change?
options: Grow about 10x, keeping tokens fixed
Grow about 5.4x
Grow about 3.2x, and tokens about 3.2x too
Stay fixed and train 10x longer
explain: $10^{0.5} \approx 3.16$ for both N and D, and $3.16 \times 3.16 = 10$ recovers the 10x compute. 5.4x is the Kaplan prescription ($10^{0.73}$) from the next lesson. Putting all of it into one knob walks up a wall of the IsoFLOP valley.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Precision, recall, and why accuracy is useless for search
question: A query has exactly 3 relevant documents in the qrels. A perfect system ranks all 3 first. What are its P@10 and R@10?
explain: Recall is 3/3 = 1.0 because every relevant document is retrieved. Precision at 10 counts all 10 slots, and only 3 can ever be relevant, so it is 0.3 even for a perfect ranking. This is why P@k is hard to average across queries with different numbers of relevant documents.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: From token vectors to one sentence vector: pooling and cosine
question: Your vectors are L2-normalized at indexing time and queries are normalized too. A teammate switches the scoring function from cosine to dot product to save time. What happens to the ranking?
options: It is identical, because for unit vectors the dot product equals the cosine
It changes, because dot product favors longer documents
It reverses
It becomes random
explain: Cosine divides the dot product by the two lengths. When both lengths are 1, that division does nothing, so the scores and the ranking are identical. This is exactly why normalizing once is standard practice.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
question: Starting from the initial corpus, suppose newest appeared 9 times instead of 6 (everything else unchanged). Which pair would be merged first?
options: (e, s), still tied with (s, t) and (t, _) at 12
(l, o), because low is the most frequent word
(w, e), which rises to 11
(n, e), because newest is now the most frequent word
explain: Each of (e, s), (s, t), (t, _) becomes $9 + 3 = 12$, and (w, e) becomes $9 + 2 = 11$. The top count is a three-way tie at 12, and the first-seen rule picks (e, s). Word frequency alone does not decide: (l, o) gets 7 and (n, e) gets 9.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Initialization: keeping signals alive through 30 layers
question: A 50-layer ReLU MLP uses weights with $\mathrm{Var}(w) = 1/\text{fan-in}$. Without normalization layers, what do you expect at initialization?
options: Activations shrink by about a factor of 2 in variance per layer, so early-layer gradients become tiny
Activations keep roughly constant scale, since 1/fan-in is the textbook choice
Activations explode because ReLU outputs are always positive
Nothing depends on initialization because Adam rescales every step
explain: Var(w) = 1/n gives g = 1, so the variance factor per layer is g/2 = 1/2. After 50 layers the variance is multiplied by about $2^{-49}$. The backward pass has the same product, so early gradients vanish. Adam rescales update sizes, but it cannot repair a forward pass whose signal has already disappeared.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: A debugging recipe: loss at init, overfit one batch, read the curves
question: Training loss keeps falling, but after epoch 12 validation loss rises steadily. What is the recipe's next move?
options: Increase the learning rate to escape the minimum
Re-initialize with He init
Regularize: more data or augmentation, dropout, weight decay, or stop early at the best validation loss
Remove model.eval() so validation uses batch statistics
explain: Diverging train and validation curves are overfitting, which is exactly what stage 4 (regularize) addresses. Early stopping on validation loss keeps the epoch-12 model while you try stronger regularization.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Tuning ef and M, and choosing between HNSW, IVF and PQ
question: You must index 1 billion 768-d vectors on machines with limited RAM. Which choice best fits the constraint?
options: HNSW,Flat, because it has the best recall versus speed
Brute force on GPUs, because it is exact
IVF with PQ codes, because each vector shrinks from 3,072 bytes to around 100
HNSW with a larger M, because more links mean less memory
explain: Raw float32 vectors alone would be about 3 TB, and HNSW,Flat needs them in RAM. IVF,PQ stores about m + 8 bytes per vector (about 104 GB with 96 codes), at some accuracy cost. A larger M increases memory, it does not reduce it.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded
question: A lab plans each new model's pretraining mix with a fixed 10T-token budget: every year it removes old human text to make room for the latest scrape, which is increasingly model-written. Which strategy from this lesson does that resemble most?
options: Accumulate, because the dataset is being refreshed
Replace, because older real data are discarded and model output takes their place
The fresh data loop, which MAD found safe in all cases
None, because a 10T-token budget is too large for collapse
explain: Holding the budget fixed while swapping out human text for model output drifts toward the replace setting, where errors compound. Keeping the original real data and growing the corpus matches the accumulate results.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: MAP_SHARED, MAP_PRIVATE and copy-on-write
question: Two worker processes map the same data file. Worker 1 uses MAP_SHARED and writes a record. Worker 2 uses MAP_PRIVATE and has only read that page. Which statement is guaranteed?
options: Worker 2 sees the new record immediately
Worker 2 never sees the new record
Whether worker 2 sees it is unspecified, so code must not depend on it
The write fails because a private mapping of the page exists
explain: mmap(2) states it is unspecified whether changes made to the file after the mmap call are visible in a MAP_PRIVATE mapping. In practice an untouched private page often still points at the page cache page, but once worker 2 writes that page it has its own copy. Use MAP_SHARED in both if they must see each other's writes.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Measuring correctly: intended start times and HdrHistogram
question: You can only sample a queue's latency once every 100 ms from a monitoring thread that blocks while sampling. One sample reads 1,050 ms. With recordValueWithExpectedInterval(1050, 100), how many values are recorded in total?
explain: It records 1050, then 950, 850, ..., 150: the loop continues while the value is at least 100, so it stops before 50. That is 1 + 9 = 10 values.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Merging overlapping roles: union, gaps and double counting
question: Roles are stored with *inclusive* end months, and the merge test is `s <= end`. One job ends in Mar 2019 and the next starts in Apr 2019. What happens?
options: They merge correctly
A spurious gap of length 0 is recorded between them, because Apr is greater than Mar
The second job is dropped
The total is 1 month too high
explain: With inclusive ends, back-to-back jobs differ by one, so `s <= end` fails and the code records a gap from Mar to Apr that contains no months. Totals still add up, but gap reports and gap filters break. Half-open intervals avoid the off-by-one entirely.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Coverage: how pass@k grows with the number of samples
question: Brown et al. find coverage on many tasks grows roughly log-linearly with k over several orders of magnitude. What best explains that shape?
options: Samples from an LLM become more accurate as you draw more of them
The benchmark mixes problems whose per-sample success rates span many orders of magnitude, so each 10x in k unlocks another slice
Temperature is raised automatically as k grows
pass@k for a single problem is linear in log k
explain: For one problem, pass@k is a sharp S-curve in log k. Averaging many such curves with offsets spread across decades smooths them into a steady rise. Samples are independent and do not get better individually.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Exchanging test-time compute for a bigger model
question: A chatbot will serve far more tokens than its pretraining corpus (R much greater than 1), and many prompts are hard for the current model. What does the evidence favor?
options: Investing in a larger or better-trained model
A large per-query test-time budget on the current small model
Majority voting with 10,000 samples
Lookahead search with a PRM
explain: With large R the FLOPs-matched test-time budget shrinks toward M, and on hard questions Snell et al. found additional pretraining more effective than test-time compute.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans: surprise, momentum and a forget gate for neural memory
question: Which change would you expect to hurt the Titans neural memory most, according to the paper's ablation?
options: Removing the persistent memory tokens
Removing the 1D convolutions after the projections
Removing weight decay (the forget mechanism)
Replacing SiLU with GELU in the projections
explain: Table 5: without weight decay perplexity rises from 27.01 to 29.04, the largest drop, with momentum next (28.98). Persistent memory matters least (27.63). The activation swap was not tested, so the paper gives no evidence for it.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Thrashing at the boundary, and why two magazines bound it at 1/M
question: A colleague proposes a single-magazine design with M = 64 instead of two magazines with M = 32, arguing it uses the same memory and has a lower 1/M. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing, a bigger M always lowers depot traffic
Magazine size must be a power of two smaller than 64
A single magazine can still thrash at its boundary: an alloc-alloc-free-free loop hits the depot on half the calls whatever M is
Two magazines double the number of locks taken per alloc
explain: The 1/M argument only holds when a depot trip leaves you with one full and one empty magazine. With one magazine, a loop straddling the empty/full boundary pays a depot trip every second operation, independent of M.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: How Linux ranks nodes into tiers: abstract distance
question: Why does the kernel compute a single *top tier* boundary instead of letting every node promote to any faster node?
options: Because pages can only migrate between nodes in adjacent tiers
Because sysfs can only show one tier
Because the top tier is always exactly one node
Because memory near CPUs is where hot pages should end up; promoting between DRAM nodes is NUMA balancing's normal job, not tiering
explain: Tier promotion moves hot pages out of slow, CPU-less memory into memory that has CPUs. Between two DRAM nodes, ordinary NUMA balancing moves pages toward the CPU that uses them. The top-tier boundary separates the two cases (node_is_toptier()).

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Holt-Winters and ARIMA: models with trend and season
question: Which statement about ARIMA and exponential smoothing is correct according to FPP3?
options: SES is equivalent to ARIMA(0,1,1), but multiplicative exponential smoothing models have no ARIMA equivalent
ARIMA strictly contains every exponential smoothing model
ARIMA cannot model seasonality
Exponential smoothing models are all stationary
explain: Linear (additive) ETS models map to ARIMA forms, for example ETS(A,N,N) to ARIMA(0,1,1). Nonlinear ETS models have no ARIMA counterpart, and all ETS models are nonstationary while some ARIMA models are stationary. Seasonal ARIMA handles seasonality with seasonal lags and differencing.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Your first kernel: program_id, offsets and masks
question: Why is BLOCK_SIZE declared as tl.constexpr instead of a normal int argument?
options: Because tl.arange needs a compile-time shape, so the value is baked into the compiled kernel
Because Python ints cannot be passed to GPU kernels
Because constexpr arguments are stored in shared memory
Because it makes the value changeable while the kernel runs
explain: Block shapes must be known when the kernel is compiled. Triton includes constexpr values in the kernel's specialization key, so each distinct BLOCK_SIZE gets its own compiled binary. Ordinary ints like n_elements are passed at run time.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Why one transformer should both read and draw images
question: Why does a unified model beat an LLM that calls a separate image generator through a text prompt, for a request like "make the dog in the previous picture wear a hat"?
options: The unified model has more parameters in total
Diffusion models cannot generate dogs
The generator only sees the prompt string, not the earlier image, while a unified model attends to the earlier image tokens directly
Tool calls are not allowed during generation
explain: The bottleneck is information, not size. In a pipeline the generator conditions only on what fits in the prompt. In a unified model the earlier image is part of the same context, so the new image can attend to it.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Evaluating unified models and choosing a design
question: A team needs one model that reads screenshots with small text and also generates images that must preserve fine detail, and can afford extra architecture. Which combination best fits the evidence in this course?
options: One shared VQ tokenizer with a causal mask, for simplicity
Discrete tokens at f = 32 to save context
A separate semantic encoder for understanding plus continuous latents with a diffusion or flow loss for generation
Text-only LLM with an external OCR tool and no image generation
explain: Chameleon's paper flags OCR as a weakness of discrete tokens, Janus shows a dedicated understanding encoder lifts MMBench from 35.0 to 69.4, and Transfusion shows continuous latents beat discrete tokens on generation at equal compute. BAGEL combines these choices.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Specializing further, and what you give up
question: An attacker finds a buffer overflow in a C web server. On a Linux VM they get code execution as the unprivileged web server user. What changes if the same server runs as a unikernel without memory protections?
options: They get code execution with full control of the VM, including raw packet I/O, with no privilege escalation step needed
Nothing: the hypervisor stops the exploit before it runs
The exploit fails because unikernels have no shell to spawn
They can immediately read the memory of other VMs on the host
explain: With one address space and one privilege level, the application is the kernel. NCC Group showed arbitrary packet I/O right after compromise. The hypervisor still confines the attacker to that VM, so other tenants remain protected unless the hypervisor itself is broken.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Graph traversal: memory layout, cache misses and prefetching
question: In the toy timeline, miss latency is 100 ns and a distance is 50 ns. Which change helps most?
options: Prefetching two or more neighbors ahead instead of one
Using AVX-512 to halve the 50 ns distance
Removing the visited-array check
Making the neighbor list longer
explain: The CPU waits because each load is issued only one distance (50 ns) before it is needed, but takes 100 ns. Issuing loads earlier overlaps more of the latency. Halving the compute time would make the stall share even larger.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: One GRPO step through RayPPOTrainer, call by call
question: You halve actor.ppo_micro_batch_size_per_gpu to fix an out-of-memory error. What happens to the learning dynamics?
options: Nothing in principle: micro-batches only split each mini-batch into smaller forward and backward passes with gradient accumulation
Each optimizer step now sees half as many responses
The number of optimizer steps per RL step doubles
GRPO groups get split across micro-batches, which corrupts the advantages
explain: Micro-batching is like gradient accumulation: it trades speed for memory. The mini-batch size, which sets samples per optimizer step, is unchanged. Advantages were already computed on the controller before update_actor, so splitting groups across micro-batches does not affect them.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Which frames to look at: uniform sampling and the needle problem
question: Why is question-aware keyframe selection awkward for a chat assistant that answers many follow-up questions about the same video?
options: Keyframes are only defined for videos under one minute
Keyframe selection cannot run on GPUs
Keyframes always contain fewer tokens than uniform frames
The selected frames depend on the question, so each new question may need a new selection pass and new visual tokens
explain: Relevance is computed against the prompt. A follow-up about a different moment needs different frames, so the encoding and prefill work is redone instead of reusing one cached representation of the video.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: World models, and why Genie learns one from unlabelled video
question: What does Genie learn from that a text-to-video model does not need, and what does it not need that classic world models do?
options: It needs only video, yet offers frame-by-frame control that video models lack
It needs action labels but not text, like classic world models
It needs text captions per frame instead of actions
It needs a hand-written game engine to generate training data
explain: Genie trains on unlabelled video only. Classic world models (Ha and Schmidhuber, Dreamer) need the action at each step; text-to-video models give control only at the level of the whole clip. Genie's latent actions give per-frame control without labels.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Rollout drift and diffusion game engines
question: In DIAMOND's Boxing experiments, one denoising step gave a blurry opponent but three steps gave a crisp one. Why?
options: One step is not enough compute to render any sprite
The opponent's moves are uncertain, so a single step averages possible futures; iterating commits to one mode
The agent's own player is also blurry for the same reason
Blur is caused by the auto-encoder, not the denoiser
explain: A one-step denoiser trained with an L2 loss outputs the mean of all plausible next frames, which blurs when the future is multimodal. The agent's own player stayed sharp because its action is known to the model. Multi-step sampling drives the sample toward one mode.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: A new head and a higher resolution
question: After loading a 224 checkpoint, you fine-tune at 384 but forget `interpolate_pos_encoding=True` in Hugging Face. What happens?
options: Training silently runs at 224 because the processor crops
The model interpolates anyway, the flag only changes the method
It fails: the 197-row position table does not fit a 577-token sequence
Accuracy is identical, because position embeddings matter little
explain: Without the flag, the HF embedding layer checks the input size and raises a ValueError (input 384*384 does not match model 224*224); the 197-row table could not be added to 577 tokens anyway. Interpolation happens only when you ask for it.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Binning: one 7-DoF action becomes seven tokens
question: Your dataset has a few teleoperation glitches with huge rotation values. Training with min-max bounds, the robot's wrist motions become jerky and imprecise. What is the most likely cause?
options: The glitches widened the interval, so normal rotations share very few, very wide bins
The LLM's vocabulary is too small to hold 256 tokens
Cross-entropy cannot be used for rotation dimensions
Binning rotations requires 512 bins by definition
explain: Outliers set the min and max, so the bin width grows and most real actions collapse into a handful of bins. This is exactly why OpenVLA bins between the 1st and 99th percentiles.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Why a transformer wants an image as a few discrete tokens
question: A tokenizer downsamples 256 x 256 images by f = 8 instead of f = 16. How long is the token sequence the transformer must model?
options: 256 tokens, because the codebook size is unchanged
1024 tokens, a 32 x 32 grid
512 tokens, because halving f doubles the length
65,536 tokens, one per pixel
explain: Each side shrinks by f, so the grid is (256/8) x (256/8) = 32 x 32 = 1024 tokens. Halving f doubles each side and therefore quadruples the token count, and the number of attention pairs grows 16x.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: FSQ and LFQ: quantizers with no learned codebook
question: Which statement about LFQ with 18 latent dimensions is correct?
options: It stores a 262,144 x 256 embedding table and searches it each step
Each token id is an 18-bit number read off the signs of the latent dimensions
It needs the VQ-VAE codebook loss to keep codes from collapsing
Two vectors with the same signs but different magnitudes get different ids
explain: LFQ quantizes each dimension to sign(z_i) and reads the id as a binary number, so 18 dimensions give 2^18 ids with no table to search. Magnitudes are discarded, and the codebook loss is inapplicable; usage is encouraged by an entropy penalty instead.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: How vLLM chooses a backend: priority lists and validation
question: On a B200 serving a DeepSeek-style MLA model you pinned `--block-size 16`. The log warns that `--block-size 16 precluded higher-priority backend(s) FLASHINFER_MLA, CUTLASS_MLA, FLASHMLA`. FLASHINFER_MLA supports block sizes 32 and 64. What fixes it?
options: Keep the flag and add `--attention-backend FLASHINFER_MLA`
Set `VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND=FLASHINFER_MLA`
Raise `--gpu-memory-utilization` so the larger blocks fit
Remove `--block-size` (or pin 32 or 64), so FLASHINFER_MLA passes validation and wins on priority
explain: A pinned block size goes into the selector config, and `supports_block_size` rejects 16 because it is not a multiple of 32 or 64. Forcing the backend while keeping 16 fails validation with a ValueError. The environment variable no longer exists. Removing the pin lets vLLM use the backend's preferred size.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Training the bridge: LLaVA's two stages and Flamingo's cross-attention
question: In LLaVA's stage 1, which parameters receive gradient updates?
options: The vision encoder only
The projection matrix only
The projection matrix and the language model
All three components
explain: Stage 1 keeps both pretrained models frozen and trains only $W$, aligning image features with the word-embedding space. Updating the LLM as well is what stage 2 does, and the vision encoder stays frozen throughout.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Why a lock-free CAS loop can starve one thread
question: A thread holds a spinlock and gets preempted for 10 ms. During that time the other 7 threads spin on the lock. Which progress class does a spinlock-protected counter belong to?
options: Blocking, because one delayed thread stops every other thread from completing
Wait-free, because each spin iteration is a bounded number of instructions
Lock-free, because the spinning threads are still executing steps
Bounded wait-free, because the preemption lasts a fixed 10 ms
explain: Lock-freedom requires that some thread completes an operation whenever threads take steps. Here 7 threads take steps and none completes, because progress depends on the preempted holder. That is the defining weakness of blocking synchronization, and the reason both lock-free and wait-free designs exist.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Making wait-free fast: fast path, slow path, and when to bother
question: You port a wait-free queue from Java to C++ for a hard real-time control thread. Which reclamation choice keeps operations wait-free?
options: Free nodes through a global mutex-protected free list
Never free nodes, but allocate each one with a malloc that may take a lock
Hazard pointers, as Kogan and Petrank propose
Defer frees until all threads pass a quiescent point, waiting if one is delayed
explain: A mutex, a locking allocator, or waiting for every thread to reach a quiescent point all let one delayed thread stall others. Michael describes hazard pointers as wait-free and usable inside wait-free algorithms without weakening their guarantee, which is why the paper suggests them.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Scoring a forecast: latitude-weighted RMSE and ACC
question: A paper reports unweighted RMSE over a lat-lon grid for a model that is accurate in the tropics but poor at high latitudes. Compared with the area-weighted RMSE, the unweighted number is likely:
options: Too pessimistic, because polar cells are over-counted
Too optimistic, because polar cells are over-counted
Identical, because weights are normalized to mean 1
Undefined, because RMSE needs a climatology
explain: Unweighted averages give each tiny polar cell the same vote as a large equatorial cell. Here the polar cells carry the large errors, so the unweighted number is inflated, just like 3.19 K versus 2.83 K in the toy grid.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: The Chase-Lev deque: two counters and one CAS
question: A thief's steal returns ABORT. What is the correct conclusion?
options: Another thread won the CAS on top; the deque may still hold tasks, so retry or try elsewhere
The victim's deque is empty, so stop trying it
The deque is corrupted and must be reset
The owner is resizing, so the thief must wait on a lock
explain: ABORT (Retry in crossbeam) only means this thief lost a race on top, against another thief or the owner taking the last task. Treating it as empty can make a worker park while work remains.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Why cosine forces you to fix the training length up front
question: A teammate evaluates the 50% checkpoint of a cosine run (T = S) and concludes that 'training on half the data gives loss X'. Why is X misleading?
options: The checkpoint has seen only half the data, so X is accurate by definition
The LR at that point is still about 0.55 of peak, so the model has not been annealed; a run with T equal to half the length would reach a lower loss
Cosine checkpoints are always better than fully trained models of the same length, so X is too optimistic
Weight decay has not taken effect yet at 50% of training
explain: Mid-run cosine checkpoints are underestimates. Most of the loss drop from annealing happens when the LR gets small, which for this run only happens near S. A cosine run with T set to the shorter length would anneal earlier and end lower.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: Where the copies go in a read and write loop
question: A server reads each file with read() into a 64 KiB buffer, then write()s it to a TCP socket. Hot files are always in the page cache. Which costs does the read/write loop add that an in-kernel transfer would avoid?
options: The DMA from disk into the page cache
Two CPU copies per byte and two system calls per chunk
The DMA from the socket buffer to the NIC
Nothing: the page cache already makes it zero-copy
explain: With hot files there is no disk DMA at all, and the NIC DMA is needed by every method. What the loop adds is the copy page cache to user buffer, the copy user buffer to socket buffer, and a read plus a write per chunk. The page cache avoids disk reads, not memory copies.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: When zero-copy pays: measurements, limits and choices
question: Kafka serves fetches with sendfile. A cluster enables TLS between clients and brokers. What happens to the zero-copy path?
options: Kafka stops using sendfile, since TLS runs in user space and the bytes must be encrypted there
Nothing, sendfile encrypts automatically
sendfile switches to splice
The broker uses MSG_ZEROCOPY instead
explain: Kafka's design docs say sendfile is not used when SSL is enabled, because the TLS library lives in user space. Kernel TLS can restore an in-kernel path, but encryption still reads every byte unless a NIC offloads it.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Evaluating zero-shot classifiers and choosing thresholds
question: An auto-tagger publishes tags without human review, and a wrong tag is costly while a missing tag is cheap. How should you set the threshold?
options: Use 0.5, since the scores are probabilities
Pick the threshold that maximizes recall
Use multi_label=False and always take the top label
On a labeled dev set, pick the lowest threshold that reaches the precision target, then confirm on a held-out test split
explain: When false positives are expensive, you constrain precision and take as much recall as that allows. 0.5 has no special meaning for these scores (T3 complaint scored 0.574 and was wrong). Always taking the top label guarantees a tag even when none applies.
